## Conclusion

The history of modern multi-agent LLM systems is not a story of steady movement from one agent to many agents. It is a story of increasing specificity about when many agents let people supervise more useful AI work.

The early wave made artificial organizations vivid. The framework wave made orchestration programmable. The evaluation wave showed that realistic agents are brittle. The skeptical wave showed that additional agents can lose to strong single-agent baselines, amplify coordination failures, or degrade artifacts. The emerging synthesis is more durable: multi-agent systems are a way to scale test-time compute into reliable work when tasks require parallel search, complementary context, specialist tools, memory, verification, human judgment, and optimized coordination.

The useful unit is not the agent. It is reliable work a human or verifier can inspect: a better patch, a stronger test, a validated extraction, a corrected memory, a trained critic, an improved routing policy, a replicated result, a safer tool action, or a clearer decision with provenance. For many real tasks, producing that work will require multiple agents. But the field's mature question is not whether multi-agent systems are good. It is what coordination structure turns extra inference into work that people can steer, audit, and integrate.

In that sense, modern LLM systems rediscover an older MAS lesson in a new medium. The medium changed from learned signals to language, tools, memory, and artifacts, but communication is still costly, local competence still does not guarantee global coordination, and reliable collective intelligence still has to be engineered through search, credit, state, verification, and training.
